title: What volatile covers, and what it did not

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, a field is declared `volatile Config config;` and one thread runs `config.value = newValue;`. What does that write give other threads?

options.text: Full visibility: a volatile reference makes each field of its object volatile
options.says: The page says only the reference config is volatile, not config.value.

options.text: Later visibility: the fields are flushed at the next read of the reference
options.says: The page says the write is not ordered by any volatile write, so no later read is promised to see it.

options.text: No ordering at all: only the reference is volatile, so they may miss it
options.says: The page says config.value is not automatically volatile and other threads may not see the write.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

questions.stem: Per this page, what made double-checked locking unsafe before Java 5?

options.text: Volatile accesses could be reordered with each other by the compiler or CPU
options.says: The page says that before Java 5 volatile accesses were already ordered among themselves.

options.text: Ordinary writes could be reordered around a volatile write, which published nothing
options.says: The page says before Java 5 ordinary reads and writes could be reordered around volatile accesses, so a volatile write could not publish other data.

options.text: Volatile reads and writes of a reference could be torn into two separate halves
options.says: The page says a single read or write of a volatile variable, including reading a volatile reference, is atomic.

concepts: Before Java 5 double-checked locking was broken even with volatile, because volatile did not order ordinary writes around it.
A volatile reference does not make the referenced object's fields volatile, so writing a field through it is not ordered.
